--- title: "Categorical Model" description: "Modeling a categorical dependent variable with more than two nominal outcomes." categories: [Classification, Regression, GLM] image: "Figures/9.png" order: 10 reading-time: true --- ## General Principles To model the relationship between a outcome variable in which each observation is a single choice from a set of more than two categories and one or more independent variables, we can use a *Categorical* model. ## Considerations ::: callout-caution - We have the same considerations as for [Regression for continuous variable](1. Linear Regression for continuous variable.qmd). - One way to interpret a *Categorical* model is to consider that we need to build $K - 1$ linear models, where $K$ is the number of categories. Once we get the linear prediction for each category, we can convert these predictions to probabilities by building a [simplex 🛈]{#simplex}. To do this, we convert the regression outputs using the [softmax function 🛈]{#softmax} (see the "jax.nn.softmax" line in the code). - The intercept $\alpha$ captures the difference in the log-odds of the outcome categories; thus, different categories need different intercepts. - On the other hand, as we assume that the effect of each predictor on the outcome is consistent across all categories, the regression coefficients $\beta$ are shared across categories. - The relationship between the predictor variables and the log-odds of each category is modeled linearly, allowing us to interpret the effect of each predictor on the log-odds of each category. ::: ## Example Below is an example code snippet demonstrating a Bayesian Categorical model using the BayesForge (BF) package. This example is based on @mcelreath2018statistical. The covariate (income) varies across individuals and careers: with the same incomes for everyone, the slope b could not be distinguished from the intercepts. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ### Python ::: {#ac0a332a .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} from BayesForge import bf import jax.numpy as jnp import jax # Setup device ------------------------------------------------ m = bf('cpu') # Simulate data ------------------------------------------------ # 300 people each choose among 3 careers; income[i, k] is the income # person i would earn in career k. Income must vary across people, # otherwise b cannot be told apart from the intercepts a. N = 300 income = m.dist.uniform(1, 10, shape=(N, 3), sample=True, seed=1) a_true, b_true = jnp.array([0.5, -0.2]), 0.4 # career 3 is the pivot scores = jnp.stack([a_true[0] + b_true * income[:, 0], a_true[1] + b_true * income[:, 1], b_true * income[:, 2]], axis=1) career = m.dist.categorical(probs=jax.nn.softmax(scores, axis=1), sample=True, seed=0) m.data_on_model = dict(career=career, inc0=income[:, 0], inc1=income[:, 1], inc2=income[:, 2]) # Define model ------------------------------------------------ def model(career, inc0, inc1, inc2): a = m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape=(2,), name='a') b = m.dist.half_normal(1.0, name='b') s_1 = a[0] + b * inc0 s_2 = a[1] + b * inc1 s_3 = b * inc2 # pivot: no intercept p = jax.nn.softmax(jnp.stack([s_1, s_2, s_3], axis=1), axis=1) m.dist.categorical(probs=p, obs=career) # Run sampler ------------------------------------------------ m.fit(model, progress_bar=False) # Optimize model parameters through MCMC sampling # Summary ------------------------------------------------ m.summary() # Get posterior distributions ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` /home/sosa/.local/lib/python3.13/site-packages/tqdm/auto.py:21: TqdmWarning: IProgress not found. ``` ::: ::: ### R ```R library(BayesForge) jax = reticulate::import('jax') jnp = reticulate::import('jax.numpy') # setup platform------------------------------------------------ m=importBF(platform='cpu') # Simulate data ------------------------------------------------ set.seed(1) N <- 300L income <- matrix(runif(N * 3, 1, 10), N, 3) scores <- cbind(0.5 + 0.4 * income[, 1], -0.2 + 0.4 * income[, 2], 0.4 * income[, 3]) p_true <- exp(scores) / rowSums(exp(scores)) career <- apply(p_true, 1, function(p) sample(0:2, 1, prob = p)) m$data_on_model <- list(career = jnp$array(as.integer(career)), inc0 = jnp$array(income[, 1]), inc1 = jnp$array(income[, 2]), inc2 = jnp$array(income[, 3])) # Define model ------------------------------------------------ model <- function(career, inc0, inc1, inc2){ a = m$dist$normal(0, 1, shape = reticulate::tuple(2L), name = 'a') b = m$dist$half_normal(1.0, name = 'b') s_1 = a[0] + b * inc0 s_2 = a[1] + b * inc1 s_3 = b * inc2 # pivot: no intercept p = jax$nn$softmax(jnp$stack(list(s_1, s_2, s_3), axis = 1L), axis = 1L) m$dist$categorical(probs = p, obs = career) } # Run MCMC ------------------------------------------------ m$fit(model) # Optimize model parameters through MCMC sampling # Summary ------------------------------------------------ m$summary() # Get posterior distribution ``` ### Julia ```julia using PyBayesForge # Setup device------------------------------------------------ m = importBF(platform="cpu") using Random # Simulate data ------------------------------------------------ rng = MersenneTwister(1) N = 300 income = 1 .+ 9 .* rand(rng, N, 3) scores = hcat(0.5 .+ 0.4 .* income[:, 1], -0.2 .+ 0.4 .* income[:, 2], 0.4 .* income[:, 3]) p_true = exp.(scores) ./ sum(exp.(scores), dims=2) career = [findfirst(cumsum(p_true[i, :]) .>= rand(rng)) - 1 for i in 1:N] m.data_on_model = Dict("career" => jnp.array(career), "inc0" => jnp.array(income[:, 1]), "inc1" => jnp.array(income[:, 2]), "inc2" => jnp.array(income[:, 3])) # Define model ------------------------------------------------ @BF function model(career, inc0, inc1, inc2) a = m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape=(2,), name = "a") b = m.dist.half_normal(1.0, name = "b") s_1 = a[0] + b * inc0 s_2 = a[1] + b * inc1 s_3 = b * inc2 # pivot: no intercept p = jax.nn.softmax(jnp.stack([s_1, s_2, s_3], axis=1), axis=1) m.dist.categorical(probs=p, obs=career) end # Run mcmc ------------------------------------------------ m.fit(model) # Optimize model parameters through MCMC sampling # Summary ------------------------------------------------ m.summary() # Get posterior distributions ``` ::: ### Posterior predictive checks Does the model reproduce how often each career is chosen? ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} #### Python ::: {#27d5d4ac .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.diag.ppc_bars() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: #### R ```r m$diag$ppc_bars() ``` #### Julia ```julia m.diag.ppc_bars() ``` ::: Bars are the observed number of people in each career, points the median predicted number with a 90 % interval. Each bar top should lie inside its interval. See [Diagnostics](start/Diagnostics.qmd) for every posterior predictive plot. ## Mathematical Details We can model a *Categorical* model using a $Categorical distribution$. The multinomial distribution models the counts of outcomes falling into different categories. For an outcome variable 𝑦 with 𝐾 categories, the multinomial likelihood function is: $$ Y_i \sim \text{Categorical}(\theta_i) \\ \theta_i = \text{Softmax}(\phi_i) \\ \phi_{[i,1]} = \alpha_1 + \beta_1 X_i \\ \phi_{[i,2]} = \alpha_2 + \beta_2 X_i \\ ... \\ \phi_{[i,k]} = 0 \\ \alpha_{k} \sim \text{Normal}(0,1) \\ \beta_{k} \sim \text{Normal}(0.1) $$ Where: - $Y_i$ is the dependent categorical variable for observation *i* indicating the category of the observation. - $\theta_i$ is a vector unique to each observation, *i*, which gives the probability of observing *i* in category *k*. - $\phi_i$ give the linear model for each of the $k$ categories. Note that we use the softmax function to ensure that that the probabilities $\theta_i$ form a [simplex 🛈]{#simplex}. - Each element of $\phi_i$ is obtained by applying a linear regression model with its own respective intercept $\alpha_k$ and slope coefficient $\beta_k$. To ensure the model is identifiable, one category, *K*, is arbitrarily chosen as a reference or baseline category. The linear predictor for this reference category is set to zero. The coefficients for the other categories then represent the change in the log-odds of being in that category versus the reference category. ## Model validation tests - [Comparison with Stan](https://github.com/BGN-for-ASNA/BF/tree/main/Test/4.%20Rethinking/Numpyro%20backend): `8.Multinomial.py` fits the same model with BayesForge and Stan and compares the posterior distributions (KL divergence). - [Documentation example](https://github.com/BGN-for-ASNA/BF/tree/main/Test/3.Documentation/Python): the Python example of this page is run by the documentation tests (`test_model_pages.py`). ## Reference(s) ::: {#refs} :::
